claims.text: Price elasticity of supply (PES) measures how strongly the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer responds when the price of the good changes; it is calculated as the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: PES is calculated by dividing the percentage change in quantity supplied by the percentage change in price; because it divides one percentage by another, the figure carries no units, and a value above 1 shows elastic supply - the quantity offered changed by a larger percentage than the price did - while a value below 1 shows inelastic supply, where the quantity offered changed by a smaller percentage than the price did.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: PES and PED share the shape of their formulas but measure opposite sides of the market: PES measures the response of the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer to a price change, while PED measures the response of the quantity buyers are willing and able to take; the test for which one applies is whose behaviour the question is about.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: To calculate PES from data: work out the percentage change in quantity supplied on its original level, work out the percentage change in price on its original level, then divide the first by the second; the result is read as elastic above 1 and inelastic below 1.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: When the wholesale price of a crate at Kaoko Juice rose from N$100 to N$110, a 10% rise, and the crates it offered each week rose from 200 to 260, a 30% rise, its PES worked out at 3: the quantity supplied responded three times as strongly, in percentage terms, as the price did, so the bottler's supply was elastic.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: On a supply diagram, price is read on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, and the steepness of the supply curve carries the elasticity: a steep curve shows the quantity offered changing little when price changes, which is inelastic supply, while a flatter curve shows the quantity offered changing a lot, which is elastic supply; when demand shifts, the same shift tends to land mostly on price where supply is inelastic and mostly on quantity where supply is elastic.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The determinants of PES are usually spare capacity - whether the seller has room to raise output without new equipment; the level of stocks - whether finished goods sit in a store ready to sell; the ease of switching production or finding extra inputs; and the length of the period the seller has to respond.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A seller with spare capacity or goods held in stock can raise the quantity offered quickly and cheaply when price rises, so its supply tends to be elastic; a seller already at full capacity with empty stores tends to show inelastic supply, because raising output takes time or new equipment.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply tends to be inelastic in the short run, because the quantity offered over the coming days is largely fixed by decisions already taken; over longer periods sellers can hire, build, plant or switch production in response to the price they have seen, so supply tends to become more elastic as the period lengthens.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A mahangu grower near Oshakati who sees a higher grain price in January cannot offer more grain that season, since the harvest was planted months before; a year later the same grower can plant more fields, which is why the grower's supply is inelastic within a season and tends to be more elastic across seasons.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: PES matters to producers because it sets what they can do with a price change: a producer whose supply is elastic can usually turn a price rise into extra sales, while a producer with inelastic supply - where the quantity offered changes by a smaller percentage than the price - may take a higher price on the same output yet cannot meet extra demand quickly.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: For consumers, inelastic supply means a rise in demand tends to land on price - shortages show up as dearer goods rather than as more of them - so markets with inelastic supply, such as housing in a growing town or fresh produce after a bad season, tend to see sharper price swings when demand shifts.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: For governments, PES shapes what policy can achieve: a subsidy or a higher guaranteed price tends to call out extra output where supply can respond, so a government hoping for more food production or more housing needs producers whose supply is elastic enough to answer the incentive.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Whether an elastic supply is the good case depends on whose position is being judged: consumers of a good in rising demand usually gain from elastic supply, because extra output rather than higher prices meets the demand, while sellers of a good in fixed supply may gain more from inelastic supply, since the shortage lands on the price they receive.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply is perfectly inelastic when PES equals 0: the quantity supplied does not change when the price changes, so the supply curve is drawn as a vertical line.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply is perfectly elastic when PES is infinite: sellers will offer any quantity at one price but none at a lower price, so the supply curve is drawn as a horizontal line.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply has unit elasticity when PES equals 1, because the quantity supplied changes by the same percentage as the price; any straight-line supply curve drawn through the origin has a PES of 1 all along it, while a straight line starting from the price axis is elastic and one starting from the quantity axis is inelastic.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
